. The Inaccessible Island rail (Laterallus rogersi) represents a remarkable example of insular evolution, being the world's smallest extant flightless bird. Endemic to a single island in the Tristan da Cunha archipelago, this species exhibits several unique life-history traits shaped by its predator-free, resource-limited environment. The incubation period for this rail is relatively extended, with embryos requiring 30 days [ab = 30 days] to complete development when maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a value consistent with metabolic rates observed in other small-bodied Rallidae during the later stages of organogenesis. Emerging from the calcareous egg, the altricial nestling weighs only 9.2 grams [Wwb = 9.2 grams] at hatching, a modest initial mass that necessitates intensive biparental provisioning throughout the early nestling phase. Reflecting the energetic constraints of its cool temperate habitat, the basal metabolic rate of adult individuals has been determined through respirometry trials to be approximately 40.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 40.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured under standard thermoneutral conditions at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C], a figure that is relatively low for a bird of its body mass and likely correlates with its flightless, energy-conserving lifestyle.

Sexual dimorphism in body size is evident in this species, with adult males attaining a greater ultimate body mass than their female counterparts. The maximum adult body mass recorded for females in a comprehensive field survey was 37.45 grams [Wwi = 37.45 grams], although some individuals may fall within a broader range of 34 to 42 grams depending on seasonal condition and reproductive status. Males, by contrast, achieve a higher asymptotic mass, with the largest documented individuals reaching 41.8 grams [Wwi = 41.8 grams], and field records indicate a typical spread from 35 to 49 grams for the heaviest birds. This level of dimorphism, while modest, is consistent with a mating system where males compete for territories and may need to defend resources against conspecifics. The growth trajectory from the neonatal mass of 9.2 grams [Wwb = 9.2 grams] to these adult values is rapid, driven by the abundant invertebrate prey available in the island's tussock grassland during the austral summer. The energetic cost of this rapid mass gain is supported by the efficient metabolic machinery reflected in the species' basal oxygen consumption rate of 40.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 40.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C].

Developmental milestones in the Inaccessible Island rail are tightly linked to the seasonal availability of resources in its subantarctic environment. Under the moderate thermal conditions typical of the breeding season, which average approximately 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] within well-insulated nests, the young birds achieve sustained flight capability at 40 days after hatching [tx = 40 days after hatching]. This fledging age, while relatively short for a rail of this size, reflects the selective pressure to reach independence before the onset of harsh winter conditions. Following fledging, the juvenile bird enters a period of somatic growth and social learning that culminates in the attainment of sexual maturity, which field observations estimate to occur at 120 days after hatching [tp = 120 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This age at puberty is notably prolonged compared to many continental rails, perhaps because the stable, low-predation environment relaxes the urgency for early reproduction and allows for a more gradual investment in tissue development. The onset of gonadal maturation marks the transition from the juvenile to the pre-reproductive subadult stage, during which individuals continue to refine foraging skills and establish territories.

Reproductive output in this species is notably constrained by the short, cool breeding season characteristic of its high-latitude island habitat. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as annual fecundity, is estimated at 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch] with approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year]. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of the nesting microhabitat, which hover near 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] due to solar exposure and parental insulation, the time since birth at first brood is approximately 511 days since birth [tR = approximately 511 days since birth]. This delay in first reproduction is ecologically significant, as it allows young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition to support the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The low annual reproductive output is compensated by an extended lifespan, with the oldest documented wild individuals reaching an age of roughly 3,905 days [am = roughly 3,905 days], equivalent to just under a decade under field conditions at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. This longevity, coupled with the modest clutch size, aligns with a slow life-history strategy typical of many oceanic island endemics.

Comparative analyses with other members of the Rallidae family reveal the extreme degree to which Laterallus rogersi has diverged from its continental relatives. Whereas most small rails produce multiple broods per season and attain sexual maturity within their first year, this species exhibits a distinctly delayed schedule. For instance, the 120 days after hatching [tp = 120 days after hatching] required to achieve puberty is roughly double that reported for the similar-sized Sora (Porzana carolina), which may mature within 60 days at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. Furthermore, the age at first reproduction of 511 days since birth [tR = 511 days since birth] is exceptionally protracted for a bird with an adult body mass of only 37.45 grams [Wwi = 37.45 grams] in females and 41.8 grams [Wwi = 41.8 grams] in males, suggesting strong selection against premature breeding in a stochastic food environment at a temperature of 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan of 3,905 days [am = 3,905 days] at 40.4 °C [T = 40.4 °C] contrasts sharply with the typical two- to three-year survival of many continental rails, underscoring the demographic consequences of predator release and the trade-off between current reproduction and survival that governs life-history evolution on remote islands.
